# Chapter Fifteen: Highland Steel

The wind coming off the North Sea carried the sharp, biting tang of salt, heather, and wet peat.

Victor stood on the crest of a rugged heather-covered knoll two miles behind the Dundee estate. Below him, the silvery expanse of the Firth of Tay gleamed beneath a canopy of low, gray Scottish clouds. His breath plumed in the cold morning air, but beneath his gray thermal shirt and canvas field pants, his skin burned with an unnatural, electric warmth.

Across from him stood Father Edgar. The burly Scottish priest had stripped down to a woolen sweater, his heavy tactical boots dug firmly into the damp turf. In his right hand, Edgar held a blunt steel training broadsword, balanced with the effortless familiarity of a man who had practiced medieval fencing since childhood.

"Again, lad," Edgar grunted, rolling his broad shoulders. "Stop thinking with your eyes. Your eyes are mortal. They're slow, clumsy, and easily fooled by mist and shadows. When a six-hundred-pound Lycan drops out of the canopy at forty miles an hour, you won't have time to register a visual contact. Feel the weight in your feet. Let the steel tell you where the strike is coming from."

Victor took a slow, measured breath. In his hands, he held the true blade: *Lobera*.

The sword was breathtaking. Two and a half feet of pristine, double-edged celestial iron, tapering to an acute, needle-like point. Down the central fuller ran intricate gold-inlaid Latin scripture, flanked by archaic Aramaic sigils that seemed to shimmer with a faint, iridescent violet hue whenever Victor's pulse quickened. The crossguard was forged from pure white gold, centered on a blood-red enameled cross that felt warm against his knuckles.

Beside it, tucked into a leather cross-draw sheath at his left hip, rested the Jamestown dagger—the very weapon that had unlocked Alfonso's memories in the Rockville safe house.

"Ready," Victor said softly.

Edgar moved with startling speed for a man of his bulk. He lunged forward, executing a vicious diagonal cut aimed straight for Victor's collarbone. The blade hissed through the cold air with lethal intent.

Two weeks ago, Victor would have flinched, backpedaled, or ended up flat on his back with a fractured clavicle. But now, as the blunt steel rushed toward him, something deep inside his neurological wiring clicked into place.

Time seemed to dilate. Victor saw the line of the blow three frames before it arrived. With an instinctive, fluid pivot on his left heel, he shifted his body six inches to the right. *Lobera* swept upward in a tight, rising parry. Steel met steel with a sharp, bell-like chime that resonated through the glen.

Without breaking momentum, Victor carried the kinetic energy through his shoulders, stepping inside Edgar's guard and bringing the flat of *Lobera*'s pommel gently against the priest's chest, while his left hand drew the Jamestown dagger and rested its blunt edge against Edgar's throat.

The entire exchange took less than two seconds.

Edgar froze, his chest heaving, his pale blue eyes wide with shock. For five silent seconds, neither man moved. Then, a booming laugh erupted from Edgar's chest, echoing off the surrounding crags.

"By Saint Andrew's cross!" Edgar roared, lowering his training sword and shaking his head in sheer disbelief. "Ten days, Victor! Ten bloody days! Most novices spend three years in the seminary just learning how not to cut off their own kneecaps, and you're disarming a third-degree Knight of the Custodes like you were strolling through a park!"

Victor stepped back, twirling *Lobera* in a clean figure-eight before sliding it smoothly back into its velvet-lined scabbard. "It isn't me, Edgar. You know that. It's the dagger. Every time I sleep, I live his battles. I feel his muscles contracting. I know how to shift my weight because he did it ten thousand times before I was even a thought."

Edgar's smile faded slightly, replaced by a solemn, contemplative expression. He reached into his coat and produced an old pewter flask, unscrewing the cap and taking a healthy swig of Glenfiddich before offering it to Victor. Victor took a small sip, welcoming the burn as it settled in his throat.

"Alfonso," Edgar muttered quietly, staring out over the misty hills. "The Lost Hunter."

Victor looked at his mentor intently. "You knew about him, didn't you? Back at the safe house, Bishop Talbot acted like the memories were a divine miracle from the Archangel Michael. But that wasn't an angel in that dagger, Edgar. It was a man. A living man who breathed the air of Virginia three centuries ago."

Edgar sighed, leaning against a weathered granite boulder. "The Vatican archives are full of convenient omissions, lad. Alfonso of Castile was King Ferdinand's direct grand-nephew. In the seventeenth century, he was the deadliest hunter the Order ever fielded. He had the genetic gift—the same pure royal bloodline you carry. When he wielded Lobera, the wolves broke like glass. But in 1612, he was deployed to the Jamestown colony to cleanse the Powhatan frontier."

"And what happened?" Victor asked.

"He vanished," Edgar said simply. "His tracking team was found slaughtered in the swamp, but Alfonso's body was never recovered. The Order declared him a casualty of war, sealed his training dagger in the vault, and struck his name from the liturgical rolls. But the older priests in the archives whispered a different story. They claimed Alfonso found something in the wilderness that shook his faith. They said he laid down his sword and walked into the forest, choosing the wolves over the cross."

Victor touched the pommel of the dagger at his hip. He remembered the raw emotion from the vision—the fear, the discipline, but most of all, the deep, agonizing conflict in Alfonso's soul when he realized that the creatures he was commanded to kill were not mindless demons, but thinking, feeling beings fighting for their families.

"Edgar," Victor said carefully, "the wolves who attacked my house... they were savages. They tried to butcher Jessica and my children. But when I was tracking that trail in Great Falls with Sam, before the attack, there was another scent. A scout. She watched me. She could have ripped my throat out in the parking lot, but she didn't. She walked away. Why?"

Edgar looked down at the grass, his jaw tightening. "Because the Lycans are not a hive mind, Victor. Like men, some are noble, and some are monsters. The pack in Rockville, led by the elder who calls himself Sowain, has maintained an unbroken truce with the East Coast dioceses for over two hundred years. They hunt deer, they live quietly, and they keep the peace. But a younger faction, led by a rabid brute named Brock, broke the covenant. Brock wants war. And I fear our own people in Rome have leaders who want exactly the same thing."

"What do you mean?" Victor pressed.

Before Edgar could answer, he straightened up, his face hardening into professional focus. "Enough philosophy for one morning, lad. If you are to survive what's coming, you need to master the command words. The ancient metallurgical artisans of Toledo did not forge Lobera for ordinary sparring. The steel is celestial iron—meteorite fallen from the heavens, annealed in sacred oils and keyed to the royal hemoglobin sequence."

Edgar stepped back and pointed his sword toward a jagged granite outcrop twenty yards away, rising four feet out of the heather.

"Draw the blade, Victor. Clear your mind. Channel the blood in your veins and speak the first word: *Bakhzataa*."

Victor drew *Lobera*. The moment the blade cleared the scabbard, he closed his eyes and inhaled the cold Highland wind. He felt the steady, rhythmic thump of his heart. In his mind's eye, he pictured the young Alfonso standing on the edge of the Virginia clearing, whispering the ancient Aramaic syllables.

"*Bakhzataa*," Victor whispered.

A sudden, electric jolt surged from the pommel into his palms. Victor opened his eyes and gasped.

The world had transformed. The gray, misty daylight was replaced by a vibrant tapestry of bio-thermal luminescence. He could see the warm, crimson pulse of Edgar's circulatory system glowing through his woolen sweater. He could see the microscopic heat trails of field mice burrowing beneath the heather forty yards away. And along the fuller of *Lobera*, the gold lettering ignited into brilliant, incandescent blue fire.

"God in heaven," Edgar whispered, stepping back in genuine awe.

"Now the second word, lad!" Edgar called out, his voice trembling with reverent excitement. "*Malka*! Focus on the stone! Release the kinetic arc!"

Victor locked his eyes on the granite boulder. He felt an overwhelming surge of kinetic resonance building along the blade's edge, humming with the frequency of a tuning fork. Stepping forward with the fluid footwork of three centuries of masters, Victor swung *Lobera* in a clean, horizontal sweep.

He did not touch the stone.

A crescent wave of brilliant silver energy detached from the sword's edge, slicing through the air with a sound like tearing silk. The silver arc slammed into the granite boulder twenty yards away.

There was no explosion, no thunderous crash. With a clean, terrifying hiss, the four-foot slab of solid granite was sheared in half. The top half slid smoothly off the base and tumbled into the heather, its cut edge glowing with faint, smoking silver heat.

Victor stood frozen, his breath catching in his throat, the sword humming gently in his hands as the blue flames slowly receded into the gold inlay.

Edgar slowly lowered his training sword, his face pale as chalk. He made the sign of the cross with a trembling hand.

"God help the wolves when you take the field, Victor," the priest whispered solemnly. "And God help us all if the butchers in Rome ever manage to take that steel from your hands."

---
